paras: The Sharkey County ambush of 1881 was the shooting of a body of Black men on their way to a Fusion political meeting in Sharkey County, Mississippi, on the night of October 28, 1881, by men hidden beside the road. Perry Thompson was killed instantly, and later accounts said two of the wounded also died. The shooters were not identified, and Mississippi papers of both parties condemned the killing as a political assassination tied to a bitter contest over county offices.

In the autumn of 1881 Sharkey County had two local tickets in the field, a straight Democratic ticket and a Fusion ticket made up of Democrats and Republicans. A Fusion meeting was called for the night of Friday, October 28, at a store on the Phelps plantation on Deer Creek, to be addressed by C. J. Jones.

A large number of Black men walking in a body along the road on the bank of Deer Creek were then "hailed by parties hid in ambush and commanded to halt." When they kept walking, the hidden men fired into them with double-barreled shotguns, killing Thompson with a shot in the back. Some suspected that the shooters had meant to kill a colored Fusion candidate and another prominent colored politician who had already passed, a theory the Globe-Democrat called "only surmise."

The first telegram from Mayersville, dated October 30, reported Thompson killed and two others dangerously wounded, and this figure ran in most papers. The Globe-Democrat account said four were wounded and two of them had since died, and the Rolling Fork resolutions and the Vicksburg Herald both spoke of three killed and two wounded.

Sheriff John S. Joor summoned a posse of citizens to go to the scene and find those responsible, and some survivors said they could identify the shooters. At an indignation meeting of white and colored men in the Rolling Fork courthouse the next day, A. D. Aldridge took the chair and declared himself willing to hunt the assassins down "though the lynch law be resorted to." Col. W. D. Brown blamed the contest between the two tickets, and the meeting resolved to use all lawful means to bring the perpetrators to punishment.

C. J. Jones told the colored people in the audience that the killing was meant to intimidate them out of a full Fusion vote and urged the survivors to rally. The Vicksburg Herald called on the governor to offer a $5,000 reward for each of the killers. The Memphis Appeal reported the assassins still at large on November 3, and the coverage shows no arrest, inquest or trial.

On November 2 the Herald's Vicksburg dispatch ran in papers from Maine to California as a one- or two-sentence item. The Daily Kennebec Journal headed it "SHOT GUN POLICY," and the Chicago Tribune ran the long Globe-Democrat special under "THE SHOTGUN POLICY. It Still Remains a Leading Feature in Mississippi Politics." The New-York Tribune put it in a Jackson dispatch on the Republican canvass under the heading "Republicans Assassinated in Sharkey County."

The Vicksburg Herald wrote of "cold-blooded, brutal, causeless murders," said the victims were inoffensive, and said the killers' purpose seemed to be to kill a number of "niggers." The Jackson Weekly Clarion said that "no cause should be upheld by such detestable and barbarous methods," and the Memphis Appeal printed a demand that the "bulldozing fiends" be hunted down and hanged.

The National Republican reprinted the Herald editorial under "COWARDLY MURDERS. The Mississippi Plan," and the Independent Statesman of Concord quoted it as the verdict of an "Independent Democrat" paper.

Accounts differ on the toll: the first Mayersville telegram of October 30, carried in most papers, gave Thompson killed and two others dangerously wounded. The Globe-Democrat said four were wounded and two had since died, and the Rolling Fork resolutions and the Herald's later editorial both gave three killed and two wounded; these later, local accounts are the fuller ones. The Superior Times dated the shooting "the 1st inst.," which matches the date of the Vicksburg wire rather than the October 28 given in every fuller account.

reader.title: Sharkey County ambush of 1881
bases: Men concealed in the bushes beside a road on Deer Creek fired shotguns into a body of Black men on their way to a Fusion political meeting, killing Perry Thompson and, by later accounts, two others (A4, A16, A17); no one was seized, accused or taken from custody.

Thompson was killed unlawfully by an unidentified, unnumbered party firing from ambush (A4, A16); the papers report no accusation, seizure or claim of justice, and attribute the killing to a contest over county offices (A17), though the Vicksburg Herald said the purpose seemed to be to kill 'a number of "niggers"' (A17, A25).

The Vicksburg Herald's Mayersville special (A16), a Globe-Democrat special (A4) and a separate Jackson dispatch (A3) independently report the ambush of Black men going to a political meeting in Sharkey County, differing only on the number killed.

framing.detail: The Vicksburg Herald called them 'cold-blooded, brutal, causeless murders', blamed a 'scramble for the county offices' and demanded the assassins be hunted down.
The Memphis Appeal headlined 'COWARDLY MURDER' and 'The Ruffianly Assassins Still at Large' and printed a call to hang the 'bulldozing fiends'.
The Jackson Weekly Clarion said 'no cause should be upheld by such detestable and barbarous methods'.
The Chicago Tribune ('THE SHOTGUN POLICY') and the National Republican ('The Mississippi Plan') presented it as Mississippi election violence.
Most papers outside the South ran the Herald wire as a one- or two-sentence item, some under 'SHOT GUN POLICY'.
